Technical Article · Genetic Engineering PROPOSED

Deterministic Grounding for Agent Software Engineering

An AI agent can pass all the tests and still deliver the wrong change. This article shows why, and how to avoid.

The agent works with what he believes he knows about the repository: context recovered, memory, a plan. If this information is no longer valid, the code may be correct in isolation and wrong for today's project, violating architecture, authorized scope or privacy.

Deterministic Grounding it is the practice of anchoring what the agent knows in a verifiable state of the repository, limiting what he is allowed to do and validating each change with recorded evidence.

What the agent believes

Request: "Add PDF export route"
Recovered context: commit C1 index
Assumption: the dependency 'pdf-kit' v1.2 is in the project
Plan: edit src/api/export.js and package. json

What the repository now has

Snapshot: commit C2 (most recent)
Lockfile: 'pdf-kit' has been removed in C2
Rule: src/api/ restricted by ADR-014 (architecture decision record)
Result: the change made on C1 conflicts with C2

Agent–Repository Gap: the agent plans on C1, but the repository is already in C2

It's like opening a Pull Request from a copy of the project a week ago: on its own, the code is correct; against what the team has changed since then, it's been born broken.

The colored seals next to the titles indicate the degree of certainty of each section: OBSERVED (observed), ESTABLISHED (established), DOCUMENTED (documented), PROPOSED (proposal) and INFERENCE (inference).

Scene 01 · The Agent–Repository Gap

Five sources of truth, each with limited authority

The error of the example above arises from treating information from different origins as if it were a single context. Each source can only assert certain things, and none can speak in the other's place. Click on each card to see what it authorizes to state and what it does not authorize.

Evidence State

Current State

Authority: The repository and the execution environment, the way they are now

Which allows you to say:

  • Tell which is the current commit, which files exist and which dependencies are installed.
  • Telling which files have changed since the last commit.

Which does NOT allow to state:

  • Tell them what the team intends to do or what the requirements will require in the future.
  • Ensure that the desired architecture is being followed. That needs a separate check.
Bastors · Case 1 · The index of two commits behind

What happened: the agent recovered the context index built in the commit C1. The repository was already in C2, where a new rule of architecture prohibits direct calls to the bank from inside the controller.

Because it seemed successful: the code generated compiles and passes the unit tests.

What no one had checked: if the index still corresponded to the current commit (C2) and whether the new layer rule was valid for the changed passage.

Lesson: A recovered index may seem consistent and outdated. Compare his commit to the current one before use.

Scene 02 · Identity of State DOCUMENTED

Snapshot Capsule: prove where the agent is looking

Think of a festival bracelet: it's for one night and a gate, you can't re-use it another day, and without it security won't let you in. Snapshot Capsule (a sealed envelope with the exact identity of the repository) does the same with the context of the agent: no recovered context reaches it without being sealed with the 7 attributes below. If one of them is missing, the whole context will be treated as unreliable.

Snapshot Identity Digest

SEALED
01. Commit SHACommit unique identifier: shows which exact version of the code the agent is viewing. a8f3d1e992b47c01
02. Branch NameWhich line of work are we in? main
03. Tree DigestProves the files match the stated commit. sha256:e3b0c44298fc1c14
04. Lockfile HashLockfile fingerprint (the file that locks the versions of the dependencies): installed ones are expected. sha256:7f83b1657ff1fc53
05. Toolchain VersionVersions of runtime and build tools. Node v22.22.1 / Vite v6.0
06. Execution EnvironmentWhere the code actually runs. Linux x86 64 Sandbox
07. Immutable Capsule DigestA hash of everything above: if any item changes, it changes. Capsule: 99a1f48b02c3

Current status: The 7 attributes are present and match the repository. The context is reliable.

Scene 03 · Contracts & Requirements PROPOSED

Prompt is not a contract

A request in natural language is an intention, not a specification that you can test. Between the need of those who asked and the proof that it was met there is a chain of transformations. It's skipping steps that requirements that seem obvious, like privacy, get lost along the way.

Human Need → Intent → Desired State → Minimum Requirement → Contract (4 Levels) → Oracle → Evidence

Oracle (oracle) is any automatic verification that gives a verdict on a property: a test, a linter (checking style and code patterns), a security scanner.

The contract is like reviewing the same Pull Request in four zooms. Each level can approve something the other would fail:

Level 1 · Interface

Does the shape match? Types, schemas, signatures of methods and message formats.

Level 2 · Behavior

You do what you promise, and that's it? Preconditions, post-conditions, invariants (which can never change) and side effects.

Level 3 · Architecture

Do you live where you should live? Layers, boundaries between modules, permitted dependencies and isolation.

Level 4 · Semantics

Is it safe and compliant? Who owns the data, privacy, retention and regulatory impacts.

Bastors · Case 2 · The metadata of the photo (EXIF) that nobody asked for

What happened: the agent implemented a photo upload service. All API tests (levels 1 and 2 of the contract) gave PASS.

Because it seemed successful: the API received and stored the photos with great response time.

What no one had checked: the implementation recorded EXIF (camera metadata, including location) on open logs and shared these metadata with third parties without consent. It's a Level Four violation.

Lesson: The main path remains green, and a side trail is left unattended because no oracle was written for it.

Scene 04 · Structural Analysis PROPOSED

Static analysis sees what is written, not what happens in execution

Static analysis (read the code without executing it) and code graphs (AST/CST, the syntactic tree of the code, plus symbols and relationships between them) form a reliable map of everything that is written. But the map does not show what only happens during execution: no static analysis captures runtime altogether.

Boundary Marker: the graph only represents what can be extracted without executing the code. Calls for reflection, eval, dynamic plugins or code generated running appear as POSSIBLE (may happen) or UNKNOWN (not known), and should never be treated as nonexistent.

Scene 05 · Governance of Action DOCUMENTED

Autonomy is not authority: Action Gateway

An advanced model can assemble complex plans on its own. That's... autonomy: how much he plans and chain actions. Authority is another thing: the permission to actually change the repository, shoot a deploy or call a privileged tool. That's the decision. Action GatewayAnd just him.

Think of it as an automatic and inflexible Pull Request reviewer: if the change touches a file outside the allowed list, it blocks, no matter how good the code is.

Low Autonomy · Low Authority

Rigid automation, local scripts and routine reading. Low risk and low capacity.

Low Autonomy · High Authority

Deploy Scripts with large radius blast (how much an error can spread) and no judgment to realize that something is wrong.

High Autonomy · Low Authority (Recommended Zone)

The agent investigates, plans and proposes. The execution is always intermediated and limited to a sandbox (insulated environment).

High Autonomy · High Authority (High Risk Zone)

The agent decides and executes directly in production: decision and execution in the same step, without barrier in the middle.

Action Gateway · the 12 steps in 3 steps

Before any real effect, each proposal passes 12 checks: understand the request (1 to 5), decide whether it is allowed (6 to 9) and execute and prove (10 to 12).

01. Receive the proposal (treated as unreliable)
02. Normalize tool and version
03. Validate the input format (scheme)
04. Solve the resources cited for their canonical names
05. Identify who is acting and in which environment
06. Check scope against list of allowed (allowlist)
07. Calculate blast radius: how much can spread if it goes wrong
08. Please refer to the Policy-as-Code rules
09. Check for approval linked to this action
10. Revalidate snapshot immediately before effect
11. Run with the minimum privilege required
12. Register the evidence and origin of everything

Diff Lens · the Gateway comparing the order with the scope allowed

[Proposed by the agent] Modify src/api/export.js and infra/deploy. yaml
[authorized scope] List of permitted: src/api/** only
[Interrupted by Gateway] Blocked: change outside the scope in infra/deploy.yaml. No effect applied.

Gateway does not only approve half of the proposal: it blocks the entire action until the scope is corrected.

Bastors · Case 3 · The writing hidden behind a reading

What happened: a non-risk reading tool (release status), is usually called. A ticket induces the agent to call inside a second tool (sync environment) which has written permission.

Because it seemed successful: the first call passes the reading check.

What no one had checked: the second call is a new action in the flow and needs to be evaluated by Action Gateway on its own. She doesn't inherit approval from the first.

Lesson: Valid format and approval of the main call do not authorize chained calls with more privilege.

Scene 06 · Epistemological Force STABLISHED

Passing the test isn't the same as being right

A test that passes (PASS) proves one thing: the property he checks was satisfied in the conditions in which he drove. It doesn't prove the system is correct or that there were no side effects. The table shows 10 types of verification (oracles), which each PASS guarantees and which remains unsecured.

The possible verdicts: PASS (passed), FAIL (failure), UNKNOWN (without basis for completion by jump test, timeout or absence of test) and CONFLICK (valid records with results incompatible with each other).

Filter by Verdict: Displaying 10 of 10 oracles (0 hidden)
Verification (oracle) Verdict Which guarantees when it passes What remains unsecured
01. Parser (syntax) PASS The entry is valid according to the grammar of the language. Right types, right meaning or working.
02. Type Checker (types) PASS Guys respect the rules of the type system. Running behavior and logic bugs.
03. Static analysis / Linter PASS The set rules and standards have been respected. That nothing is missing and that there is no functional regression.
04. Unit test PASS The case tested passed with the inputs used. Border cases that no one has written and forgotten requirements.
05. Integration test PASS The components worked together in the tested scenario. Behavior under a lot of competition or production.
06. Security Scanner PASS No known vulnerability was found. Business logic failures that have never been catalogued.
07. Runtime Monitor UNKNOWN The metrics were normal in the observed window. What happens outside this window, like at peak times.
08. Model Checker (formal model) FAIL The formal model respects invariants. That the model faithfully represents the real code.
09. Formal Checker CONFLICK Mathematical proof that the code matches the specification. That the specification captures what the person really wanted.
10. Human Review PASS One person assessed and approved the change, according to his judgment. Protection against something the person missed.
Bastors · Case 4 · The test that disappeared instead of the bug

What happened: the test test rejects negative amount() failure after a change. For the suite to pass again, it is marked with skip (jumping)

Because it seemed successful: The test suite is 100% green, with no fault in sight.

What no one had checked: the coverage of what should be tested decreased. The skip hides the gap instead of solving it.

Lesson: Less failed testing does not mean more correct software. It can mean just less being watched.

Scene 07 · Auditability STABLISHED

Evidence Record: the receipt of each validation

All validation should generate a Evidence Record Unchangeable. It does not only keep the result: it records where it came from (the provenance), which version of the validator ran, in which environment and what remained outside. It's a receipt, not a certificate: proof that you passed that test in those conditions, and you don't guarantee that anything will break after.

Record ID: ev 8f9a2b01c4 VERDICT: PASS

Target (URI Subject): git://repo@a8f3d1e/src/api/export.js

Commit: a8f3d1e992b47c01

Request: REQ-EXPORT-001

Verification (oracle): orc nodest v22 (integration test)

Executor (validator): Node-test-runner:v22.22.1

Implementation environment: Docker Sandbox / isolated network

What was out: 88% of the covered lines / EXIF logging NOT covered

Origin Signature (Provinance): sig: sha256:990a1f...

Notice the highlighted field: the record states the blind spot itself. Here, PASS with 88% coverage says nothing about Case 2 EXIF logging.

Scene 08 · Decision & Closing PROPOSED

From evidence to decision, and where to start

Reconciliation is the time to decide what to do with change. It compares the desired state, the current state, the evidence obtained and the policy rules, and produces one of seven possible decisions, not only accept or reject.

01. Desired State

Acceptance requirements and rules that can never be broken.

02. Current State

The diff (the difference between the code before and after) of the repository after the agent action.

03. Evidence State

The Evidence Record, with verdicts and limits.

04. Policy State

The list of permissions and approvals of the action.

The 7 possible decisions

1. Accept change: The evidence is enough and everything is within politics.
2. Block change: There was a scope breach or a verification failed.
3. Request human review: the impact is high or there is uncertainty.
4. Start new cycle: The agent adjusts the plan and tries again.
5. Correct verification: the test is unstable (flaky) or is wrong.
6. Change specification: a person explicitly decides to change the requirement.
7. Time-limit exception: temporary release, accompanied and date to end.

Experiment: What if you turn off a control?

Turn off the mechanisms below and see which of the 5 classes of deviation (invented dependence, outdated context, out-of-scope change, violation of architecture and divergent status of the repository) are back to unprotected. Each class depends on at least one control, and the violation of architecture depends on two (validation and grounding).

All five detour classes are protected.

Start with an MVA (Minimum Viable Architecture)

An MVA is the smallest version of the pipeline worth running. Mount him with a low risk, following these seven actions:

  1. Choose a small, low-impact task.
  2. Fix Snapshot Capsule (the commit SHA, tree digest and lockfile hash).
  3. Declar in Action Gateway the list of allowed and prohibited files.
  4. Turn at least one requirement into a contract, with an independent oracle to verify it.
  5. Turn the agent in a sandbox, without any implied authority.
  6. Register PASS, FAIL, UNKNOWN and CONFLICK verdicts at Evidence Record.
  7. Compare the result with a baseline (the same task without grounding).
Start with Snapshot Capsule

Scene 09 · Glossary

The terms, in common language

The original terms remain correct and appear throughout the article. This table is the shortcut to remember what each one means.

Original term In common language Which means
Agent–Repository GapMisalignmentThe difference between what the agent believes to know about the repository and what's really there now. In academic texts appears as G t = A t − S t, where A t is what the agent assumes in instant t and S t is the actual state of the repository at this instant.
Snapshot CapsuleThe context sealSealed envelope that proves which commit and what environment the agent is viewing.
Action GatewayThe Pull Request inflexible reviewerThe barrier that decides what the agent can actually execute.
AllowlistList of permissionsOnly what's on the list can be touched. The rest is blocked.
Policy-as-CodeRule written as codeVersioned permitted and prohibited rules, instead of a PDF policy that nobody consults.
Blast radiusDamage radiusHow much action can spread if it goes wrong.
Oracle (oracle)Automatic verificationAny automatic check that gives a verdict on a property: test, linter, scanner.
Evidence RecordThe validation receiptUnchangeable record of what was checked, by whom and under what conditions.
Coverage BoundaryWhat was left out of the testThe explicit limit of what validation did not cover.
ProvenanceSource TrackThe checkable chain of who generated and signed evidence.
Desired StateWhat should be trueDeclared acceptance requirements and criteria.
Current StateWhat's true nowThe observable status of the repository at this time.
Contract of 4 levels4 zoom revisionInterface, behavior, architecture and semantics. Each level can approve what another would fail.
Autonomy vs. AuthorityThinking alone vs. being able to executeWhen the agent plans without help, against how much he can really change.
ReconciliationThe final decisionStage that joins requirement, state, evidence and politics and decides the next step.
MVA (Minimum Viable Architecture)The least it's worth rollingThe smallest version of the governance pipeline that already brings benefits.

In short

What is Deterministic Grounding

A development agent can produce syntactically correct code, pass isolated tests and still violate the architecture, authorized scope or actual status of the repository. Deterministic Grounding establishes explicit state anchoring, authority limitation by Action Gateway and validation with auditable oracles.

  • Agent–Repository Gap — the difference between what the agent believes to know about the repository and what is really there now.
  • Snapshot Capsule — immutable envelope that seals commit, tree, lockfile and environment before action.
  • Action Gateway — 12-step barrier preventing execution outside the scope (Diff Lens and allowlist).
  • Evidence Record — registration with bounded verdicts (PASS, FAIL, UNKNOWN, CONFLICT) and observation borders.

Integrates the journey of Trust Engineering and AI Agent Engineering.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Agent–Repository Gap?

It is the difference between what the agent believes to know from the repository (memory, recovered context, plan) and what can be verified in it now (current commit, dependencies, current rules). The greater the difference, the greater the risk of a change that seems right and not.

Why does a green test result (PASS) not guarantee global correction?

Because an oracle (an automatic check) tests only one specific property under a restricted execution envelope. He does not observe collaterals out of its scope, privacy leaks or unmapped architectural violations in the test.

What is Snapshot Capsule?

It is the immutable envelope containing commit SHA, branch, tree digest, lockfile, toolchain, execution environment and a unique digest that ensures that the agent context corresponds exactly to the repository state.

What's the difference between Autonomy and Authority?

Autonomy is the ability of the model to plan and chain actions flexibly; Authority is the effective permission to produce effects on the repository, which must be restricted and mediated by Action Gateway.
